metadata.title: Solving the paradox between the generalized partial credit model and PISA’s rating instructions: A generalized IRTree approach to within-rating multidimensionality

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study re-analyzed the PISA 2022 Creative Thinking dataset at the item-response (rater-mediated) level, recoding each trichotomous item into two sequential node variables (node 1: any credit vs none; node 2: full credit vs partial, conditional on passing node 1). The analytic sample included respondents with at least one response on the retained ordinal items (142,431 respondents), after excluding items scored on a binary scale and excluding respondents with completely missing responses across the retained items. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, it is unclear whether estimates were population-representative under PISA’s sampling design. Because the models are estimated via EM for IRT-style response trees (mirt) and the paper does not discuss weighting, the safest interpretation is that the analysis likely proceeded without explicit survey-weight incorporation, which may affect standard errors and uncertainty quantification under the clustered sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not analyzed directly in this paper because the authors explicitly operate at the level of item responses and rating processes (node-level decisions) rather than downstream PISA scale scores or PV-based achievement. The dependent variables are the recoded node outcomes derived from the ordinal rater scores (0/1/2 mapped to node 1 and node 2), so PV generation/combining is not part of the estimation target. Missing-data handling is not reported in terms of an imputation or deletion rule beyond the exclusion of respondents with completely missing responses across the retained items; the paper does not specify how partially missing node observations were treated in the likelihood estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Re-analysis of PISA 2022 Creative Thinking item responses from the OECD public dataset. Items scored on a binary scale were excluded because the IRTree models are not applicable to those items. This produced three item subsets: 8 items for Generate Diverse Ideas (GDI), 11 items for Generate Creative Ideas (GCI), and 9 items for Evaluate and Improve Ideas (EII). The analytic sample comprised respondents with at least one item response on the remaining ordinal items, excluding respondents with completely missing responses across these items (rotated booklet design implies missingness across item subsets). The authors pooled across countries and assumed measurement invariance as a pragmatic modeling choice; no country-level inclusion/exclusion criteria were described.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict science performance, finding that This paper re-analyzed PISA 2022 Creative Thinking rater-mediated trichotomous scores (no credit/partial/full) at the item-response level, focusing on whether the generalized partial credit model’s within-rating unidimensionality assumption is consistent with OECD rating instructions. The authors excluded binary-scored items and recoded each ordinal item into two sequential node decisions, then estimated generalized item response tree (IRTree) models: a within-rating unidimensional baseline (Tutz sequential model) and within-rating multidimensional specifications aligned to the scoring rubric (appropriateness at node 1; originality/diversity at node 2, conditional on passing node 1). Model fit comparisons used AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HQ, with multidimensional models outperforming unidimensional ones for EII and GCI and showing an overall better fit pattern across subtests. Reliability was lower for node-2 traits (originality/diversity) than for node-1 traits (appropriateness), and latent traits correlated strongly with each other and with PISA mathematics, reading, and science performance. Limitations include the lack of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that the study evaluates measurement-model assumptions rather than PV-based score validity directly. data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the study is primarily a psychometric measurement-model comparison (generalized IRTree vs unidimensional Tutz sequential model) rather than a predictive ML pipeline with supervised targets, train/test evaluation, or ML algorithms as defined in the schema. Consequently, there are no ML techniques to list under the ML-only constraint, and no predictive target-variable rows with accuracy/RMSE/AUC-style metrics. The paper does provide quantitative psychometric model-fit indices (AIC/BIC/SABIC/HQ), latent correlations, and reliability estimates, which are captured in the narrative outcome summary rather than in main_findings rows.
